chunks.text: Alstonia scholaris belongs to the dogbane family Apocynaceae. Linnaeus first described it as Echites scholaris in 1767; Robert Brown moved it into the genus Alstonia (named for botanist Charles Alston) in 1810. The species name 'scholaris' refers to its wood once being used for school writing-slates and blackboards in Myanmar. It is a large evergreen tree, occasionally reaching 40 metres (rarely up to 60 m), with narrow buttresses running up the trunk that give it a fluted look, and grey, lenticel-dotted bark. Every part of the tree exudes copious white latex when cut. Glossy dark green leaves are arranged in whorls of four to eight (the 'seven leaves' of its common name refers to this whorled habit), and it bears small, strongly scented, cream-white tubular flowers in branched clusters at the branch tips, followed by long, slender, paired seed pods up to 30 cm long. It is native across a very wide belt from Pakistan through the Indian subcontinent, Sri Lanka, Indo-China, Malesia, New Guinea and into northern Australia, growing from sea level to over 1,000 m in habitats ranging from rainforest to savannah. The IUCN lists it as Least Concern.

Traditionally, saptaparni bark has been used across Asia as a bitter tonic for gastrointestinal complaints, chronic diarrhoea, advanced dysentery, and general debility following fever, and was classed as an astringent, anthelmintic and antiperiodic remedy. However, modern pharmacological studies have found only limited efficacy against malaria (Plasmodium falciparum) or intestinal parasites such as Giardia and Entamoeba histolytica, despite its historical reputation. The bark and other parts contain a range of indole alkaloids — including echitamine (the principal toxic compound), ditamine, alstonine, echitenine and strictamine in the bark, and picralinal in the leaves — and animal studies show dose-dependent organ toxicity that varies with the season of harvest (bark cut in the monsoon is least toxic; summer-harvested bark is most toxic). This gap between long traditional use and thin modern evidence, combined with documented toxicity, means the plant should not be treated as a proven home remedy.

The soft, fast-grown timber has long been used for pencils, coffins (in Sri Lanka), net floats and household utensils (in Borneo), and cork substitutes. The tree carries considerable cultural weight in South Asia: it is the state tree of West Bengal, where it is called 'chhatim', and is revered in Jainism as the sacred tree associated with Ajitnatha, the second Tirthankara. Visva-Bharati University, founded by Rabindranath Tagore, awards a saptaparni leaf to graduating students as a symbol of learning — originally one leaf per student, now a single leaf representing the whole graduating class for conservation reasons. In Vietnam, where it is called 'hoa sua' (milk flower), its autumn blossom is a recurring image in poetry and song, though its heavy night-time fragrance has also provoked local disputes over street-tree planting (notably in Tra Vinh province in 2011). Theravada Buddhist tradition also associates the tree with the Buddha's enlightenment.
